title: Help Your Middle Managers Be Better—Jellyfish?
author: Mattson, Craig
summary: Mattson, writing as a guest post, uses a botched meeting where he had to defend an unpopular performance-review policy change to argue that senior leaders equip middle managers wrong. He extends a jellyfish metaphor — tough, flexible survivors rather than spineless creatures — to argue managers need 'the right kind of pressure internally' rather than exhortations to just be blunt. Drawing on self-determination theory, he organizes his advice around three needs: respecting a manager's autonomy (their role has its own distinct logic), equipping their competence (not just to convey information but to persuade skeptical audiences), and reinforcing their relatedness (senior leaders should sometimes physically show up in hard meetings). The piece's real target is a common executive mistake: assuming a manager's job is just to relay a decision efficiently, when the harder job is helping people process a decision they're suspicious of. It ends by rejecting the demand that middle managers simply 'be more blunt' as fundamentally miscast.
points: Middle managers stuck between skeptical peers and senior leadership need internal support (autonomy, competence, relatedness), not external pressure to be more direct.
A manager's role isn't a smaller, less-empowered version of an executive's — it has its own distinct logic senior leaders need to understand.
Persuading skeptical audiences takes more than clearly conveying information — it requires anticipating and naming their specific objections in advance.
Asking people affected by a policy to rate their own feelings about it (a deep-canvassing technique) surfaces resistance productively instead of debating it away.
Senior leaders showing up in person for a manager's hardest meetings does more for that manager's standing than any coaching conversation afterward.
quotes: But because your role entails lots of resolve and decisiveness, it's easy to treat everybody else's role as if that's what their work is like too. All they need, in other words, is directness and resoluteness.
Their role isn't just a smaller and less-empowered version of yours. Their role has its own indispensable way of standing within your organization.
But they don't just need competence in conveying information; they also need it for convincing people. And sometimes they themselves need convincing.

Following the example of deep canvassers like Dave Fleischer, you might coach your manager to ask, "On a scale of 1 to 10, how do you feel about the new policy?" That question gets their feelings out in the open, not so the manager can attack or avoid them, but so that skeptical employees can begin to query their own feelings.

If my higher-ups had been in my meeting, they might have simply counseled me to be more blunt, forceful, direct, terse. But that advice is roughly equivalent to telling a jellyfish to imitate a hammerhead.
They have complexly evolved identities that need your help to stay both firm and supple, flexible and strong, in the changeful conditions of leadership today.
